title: Syria ruled through diplomacy before empires tried to rule through Syria
dek: Around 2300 BCE, when Ebla signed peace treaties with neighbors, even the feeding protocol for a waiting messenger was written law—Syria didn't just participate in diplomacy, it invented the rules.
why: A dense ancient Near Eastern overview from Ebla to Mitanni, loaded with cases and figures; best heard straight through rather than hopping between chapters.
who: Readers interested in ancient Near Eastern history, diplomacy's origins, and long-distance trade networks—especially those curious how peripheral powers shaped great-power rivalry.
skip: The first ~2 minutes of show promotional material.

points.h: Syria built wealth on sheep and looms, not on gold it never mined
points.body: Syria had no gold or silver deposits, yet Ebla's kings commanded herds of roughly 80,000 sheep. They mobilized armies of weavers to produce high-grade textiles in different qualities and colors—each a status marker. These fabrics were stored in dedicated treasuries, carried as diplomatic gifts when the king visited distant courts, then traded back for gold, silver, and gems. In short: this inland kingdom's wealth rested not on ore but on pastoral scale and textile diplomacy.

points.h: The first diplomatic letters encoded three rituals that would reshape statecraft
points.body: An official's letter from the reign of Ilkabum-Damu is among the oldest known diplomatic documents. The officials addressed each other as ‘brother,’ a word choice signaling equal status—vassals would have used ‘father-son’ language instead. The letter naturally included three elements: an envoy, a written message, and a gift. The tone suggests this was already standard practice, not a novel invention, meaning oral diplomatic protocols likely operated long before any of it was written down.

points.h: The oldest peace treaty dictated protocol down to feeding a waiting messenger
points.body: The Treaty of Abarsal, signed around 2300 BCE, is the oldest known peace treaty. The signatories were not equals—one was plainly subject to Ilkabum-Damu—yet the treaty included a telling detail: if the other side's messenger waited at court for more than ten days awaiting a reply, the host was obliged to feed him. Such clauses reveal that diplomatic protocol was already highly institutionalized. Nations knew how long an envoy typically waited, how he should be treated, and that written procedures existed to settle disputes outside of war.

points.h: A father's letters proved his musically gifted heir was not fit to rule
points.body: Shamshi-Adad divided his kingdom into three parts, sending two sons to rule as regional governors. His younger son, Yashmah-Addu, was posted to Mari and performed poorly. His father's surviving letter is brutal: he scorned the boy for having no beard, questioned whether he was even a man, and raged that he had not properly housed the foreign princess sent to marry him. Yet the letter's own details suggest a different picture: Yashmah-Addu preferred music and feasting to warfare—not incompetent, but simply not the military heir his father demanded.

points.h: Why Hammurabi suddenly burned the one kingdom he had treated as equal
points.body: Zimri-Lim and Hammurabi had exchanged envoys and gifts, supported each other's armies, and forged a close alliance. Then Hammurabi marched north, destroyed Mari's palace, and carefully extracted the archive's most important documents before setting fires that consumed the rest—a calculated act that looks planned, as though negotiated in advance. Scholars speculate that Zimri-Lim died without an adult heir and that Mari's leadership asked Hammurabi to govern temporarily; he gradually shifted from regent to conqueror. But the true motive remains unexplained.

points.h: Cloves from Indonesia in Syria proved ancient trade routes were far larger
points.body: In a storage room of an ordinary house at Tell Kahat, archaeologists found a few grains of cloves—a spice that only grows in Indonesia. This is the westernmost and earliest-known evidence of clove dispersal, pushing back the date by centuries. But only a handful of grains were present, no intact cargo or any written record of Indonesian merchants making the journey. This points to a chain of hand-to-hand transfers, station by station, proving that a trade network far larger than previously imagined already existed.

points.h: The entire ancient world entered a recording void at almost the same time
points.body: Around 1595 BCE, the Hammurabi dynasty ended in Babylon. At nearly the same moment, written records across Mesopotamia and Syria abruptly ceased—only a handful of kingdoms like Hana left behind scattered documents. This ‘dark age’ does not mean civilization collapsed or declined, only that few writing materials survived. Scholars once suspected a dating error, but evidence confirms the gap is real: historical documentation simply becomes scarce.

points.h: Egypt abandoned conquest and adopted the diplomatic system it could not defeat
points.body: Egypt's New Kingdom initially pursued northward expansion by force. Under Thutmose III, gifts from other kingdoms were branded as ‘tribute.’ But by Amenhotep II's reign, Egypt halted its war against Mitanni and instead formalized unions through marriage and peace treaties. Both sides had discovered that the other was too large to truly swallow. Egypt then adopted wholesale—letter-perfect, with no modifications—the Mesopotamian diplomatic system that had originated in Syria: Akkadian-language correspondence, mutual envoys, and the exchange of gifts.
